summary.text: The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains the Solar System, named for the hazy band of light it makes across the night sky.
Its innermost stars form a bulge from which a bar radiates, which makes it a barred spiral galaxy.
Until the early 1920s most astronomers thought it held every star in the universe, until Hubble's observations in 1923 showed it is one of many galaxies.

items.prompt: On a dark night you see a pale, hazy stripe across the sky instead of separate points of light. Why does it look hazy?

Its stars are so far off that the naked eye cannot separate them
Its stars are too dim to give off any light at all

Black holes swallowing the light of stars behind them
Areas where interstellar dust blocks light from distant stars

paragraphs.heading: Our home galaxy
paragraphs.text: The Milky Way is the galaxy that holds the Solar System. Its name comes from how it looks from Earth: a pale, hazy band of light, about 30° wide, arching across the night sky. That glow comes from countless stars and other material lying along the plane of the galaxy, too far off for the naked eye to pick out one by one. Every star you can see without a telescope belongs to the galaxy, but the name Milky Way is kept for the band itself.

paragraphs.heading: One galaxy among many
paragraphs.text: In 1610 Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at the band and saw it split into separate stars. Even so, until the early 1920s most astronomers believed the Milky Way held every star in the universe. After the 1920 Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Doust Curtis, Edwin Hubble's observations in 1923 showed it is just one galaxy of many.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and size
paragraphs.text: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy. The stars in its innermost 10,000 light-years form a bulge, and a bar stretches out from it. The main body is estimated at about 87,400 light-years across, while a surrounding region of dark matter may reach close to 2 million light-years. At the center sits Sagittarius A*, a strong radio source that is a supermassive black hole of about 4.1 million times the Sun's mass. The Solar System lies on the inner edge of the Orion Arm, some 27,000 light-years from the center.

paragraphs.heading: Stars, history and neighbours
paragraphs.text: The galaxy is thought to contain 100 to 400 billion stars, and at least as many planets. Its oldest stars probably formed soon after the Dark Ages of the early universe. They first took a spherical shape, and later the galaxy flattened into a spiral disk where newer generations of stars were born. The Milky Way has several satellite galaxies and belongs to the Local Group, which sits within the Virgo Supercluster, itself part of the Laniakea Supercluster.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing it in the sky
paragraphs.text: The band is far from smooth. Brighter soft patches called star clouds lie along it, and the most striking is the Large Sagittarius Star Cloud, part of the galaxy's central bulge. Dark stretches such as the Great Rift and the Coalsack are places where interstellar dust blocks the light of more distant stars. Its surface brightness is fairly low. Background light, such as light pollution or moonlight, can make it much harder to see.

paragraphs.heading: Stories and names
paragraphs.text: People have read the band in many ways. In one Greek myth, Zeus sets the infant Heracles at the breast of the sleeping Hera so he will become immortal; she wakes, pushes the unknown baby away, and her spilled milk forms the Milky Way. Several Uralic, Turkic and Baltic languages call it the Birds' Path, and northern peoples noticed that migrating birds follow its course. Across East Asia it is the Silver River, and Swedes call it Winter Street, as it shows most clearly in the northern winter.
